name: North Sikkim
tagline: Lachung, Lachen, Yumthang and the high lakes near Tibet
summary: North Sikkim is the high, permit-controlled part of the state above Mangan, reached on 2–3 night trips from Gangtok. People come for the Yumthang valley and its rhododendrons, snow at Zero Point, and Gurudongmar Lake at about 5,430 m. Go March to May or October to November, and check road status first.
meta_description: North Sikkim travel: Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen, Gurudongmar Lake and Dzongu. Permits, altitude, road status, costs and honest 2–3 night trips from Gangtok.
intro: North Sikkim is the largest and least crowded district of Sikkim, now officially called Mangan district. It runs from the warm Teesta gorge at Mangan, under 1,000 m, to the cold desert plateau on the Tibetan border above 5,000 m. Two valleys carry almost all visitors: the Lachung valley to the north-east, with Yumthang and Zero Point, and the Lachen valley to the north-west, with Thangu and Gurudongmar Lake.

Almost everyone visits on a short package from Gangtok, because the area is restricted. Indian travellers need a permit arranged by a registered tour operator, and foreigners need a Protected Area Permit and can only go as far as Yumthang on the Lachung side. You cannot drive your own car or go alone. The usual trip is two nights in Lachung, or three nights covering Lachen and Lachung together.

The roads are the hard part. On 4 October 2023 a glacial lake outburst sent a flood down the Teesta, damaging the Chungthang dam, bridges and long stretches of the North Sikkim highway. Repairs have gone on since, and monsoon landslides have closed the area for days or weeks at a time. Routes, permits and the Lachen–Lachung link can change at short notice. Check current status before you travel.

For the slower traveller there is Dzongu, a Lepcha reserve on the west bank of the Teesta below Mangan. It sits much lower, at roughly 700–2,000 m, with cardamom groves, waterfalls and village homestays. It needs its own permit but has none of the altitude risk, and it pairs well with a night or two in the high valleys.

highlights.title: Yumthang valley in spring
highlights.text: From mid-April to May the valley floor at 3,564 m turns pink and red with rhododendrons inside the Shingba sanctuary.

highlights.title: Gurudongmar Lake
highlights.text: A sacred glacial lake at about 5,430 m, open to Indian travellers only, reached at dawn from Lachen.

highlights.title: Snow at Zero Point
highlights.text: Yumesamdong, about 23 km above Yumthang, usually has snow from November to April and is the end of the road for tourists.

highlights.title: Lachung and Lachen villages
highlights.text: Two wooden Bhutia villages run by their own traditional councils, the Dzumsa, with monasteries above the rooftops.

highlights.title: Lepcha homestays in Dzongu
highlights.text: A protected Lepcha reserve where you stay in family homes, walk to waterfalls and eat local food.

highlights.title: The drive up the Teesta
highlights.text: Waterfalls, gorges and suspension bridges between Mangan, Chungthang and the high valleys make the long road part of the trip.

facts: Bagdogra (IXB), about 125 km to Gangtok, then 5–7 hours north
Nepali, Sikkimese (Bhutia), Lepcha, Lachungpa and Lachenpa dialects, Hindi
Permit via registered operator for Indians; PAP for foreigners, Yumthang limit
people: The high valleys are home to the Lachungpa and Lachenpa, Bhutia communities who speak their own Tibetic dialects, follow Tibetan Buddhism and have long herded yaks and traded across the passes. Each village is governed by its own Dzumsa, a council headed by an elected Pipon, which the state recognises in place of a panchayat. Lower down, Dzongu is a reserve for the Lepcha, the oldest known inhabitants of Sikkim, who call themselves Rongkup and keep both Buddhist and older Bongthing and Mun traditions. Nepali-speaking families live along the Teesta road at Mangan and Chungthang. Ask before photographing people or prayer rooms, and follow village rules on noise and plastic.

budget_day.covers: per person per day: a seat on a shared group tour from Gangtok, a homestay or simple lodge room shared by two, all meals, and the permit fee
per person per day: a reserved car shared by two, a good hotel in Lachung or Lachen with meals, permits and the driver's costs
per person per day: a newer SUV for two, the best rooms on the route with heating, all meals, permits and the Zero Point add-on

months.weather: Very cold, -5 to 8°C in Lachung, snow likely
months.summary: Lachung is open in most years and Yumthang lies under snow. The Gurudongmar road often closes after heavy snowfall, so treat it as a bonus rather than a promise.
months.tip: Bring proper thermals and gloves; most rooms have only electric blankets or a small heater.

months.weather: Cold and mostly clear, snow on the passes
months.summary: Snow is reliable at Zero Point and often reaches Yumthang. Losar falls in February or early March and villages celebrate quietly at home and in the monasteries.
months.tip: Keep a spare day in case the road above Lachung shuts after fresh snow.

months.summary: Snow melts slowly from Yumthang while Zero Point stays white. Roads reopen to Gurudongmar as the month goes on, depending on the season.
months.tip: Ask your operator whether the Gurudongmar road is open before choosing Lachen.

months.weather: Cool and fresher, showers in the afternoon
months.summary: The rhododendrons begin flowering at Yumthang from mid-April. This is one of the two best months, and also one of the busiest.
months.tip: Book Lachung rooms early for Easter and the Bengali New Year holidays.

months.summary: Peak rhododendron season and peak crowds, with school holidays filling the valleys. Gurudongmar is usually open and the lake begins to thaw.
months.tip: Leave Lachung for Yumthang by 6 am to beat the line of jeeps.

months.summary: Rain sets in and landslides can close the road for days, sometimes trapping visitors. Permits are often suspended during heavy rain.
months.tip: If you must go, buy travel insurance and keep two spare days at the end.

months.weather: Heavy rain, cloud on the valleys
months.summary: The wettest month. Tourist permits for the high valleys are often suspended, and views are rare even when the road is open.
months.tip: Plan West Sikkim or Darjeeling instead and come back in October.

months.weather: Wet, warm in the gorge, cold above 3,000 m
months.summary: Still monsoon, with frequent closures. Alpine flowers bloom above Yumthang when the cloud lifts, but the road risk is high.
months.tip: Watch the Sikkim government and police notices for road updates.

months.weather: Rain easing late in the month
months.summary: The monsoon weakens and permits usually resume, though landslide repairs can slow the drive. Late September can be green and quiet.
months.tip: Allow for one-way convoy timings at repaired stretches.

months.summary: Autumn brings the clearest skies and steady roads. It is busy during the Puja holidays, so book well ahead.
months.tip: Gurudongmar is at its bluest now; dress for a hard wind at the lake.

months.summary: Very good visibility, thinner crowds and first snow at Zero Point. Nights in Lachen drop below freezing.
months.tip: This is the best month for good-value rooms with clear views.

months.summary: Lachung and Yumthang may get snow, and Christmas brings a holiday rush from Kolkata. Gurudongmar access depends on snowfall.
months.tip: Ask for a room with a heater and confirm whether it costs extra.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then drive 114–125 km to Gangtok in 4–5 hours. North Sikkim trips start from Gangtok, where operators arrange permits and vehicles. From Gangtok the road runs north through Kabi, Phodong and Mangan (67 km, about 3 hours) to Chungthang, where it splits: Lachung is about 120 km and Lachen about 125 km from Gangtok, each 6–8 hours depending on road repairs. Shared jeeps run from Gangtok to Mangan for Dzongu. Since the October 2023 flood, some stretches run on temporary roads or one-way timings. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian citizens need a permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen and Gurudongmar, applied for by a registered Sikkim tour operator with your photo ID and photographs; you travel in a registered vehicle with that operator. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Inner Line Permit to enter the state plus a Protected Area Permit for North Sikkim, in a group of two or more through a registered agent, and may go only as far as Lachung, Yumthang and Lachen. Gurudongmar and Zero Point are closed to foreigners. Dzongu needs a separate permit, usually arranged through your homestay. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Two nights from Gangtok covers Lachung, Yumthang and, if open, Zero Point. Three nights lets you add Lachen and Gurudongmar Lake. Add two nights in Dzongu if you want a calm, low-altitude village stay. Count one more day for Gangtok on each side, as you arrive from Siliguri and need a night there while the operator arranges permits.

faqs.q: Can I travel to North Sikkim on my own?
faqs.a: Not fully. Permits for Lachung, Lachen and the lakes are issued only through registered tour operators, and you must travel in a registered vehicle. You can choose a shared group tour, which is the cheapest, or a reserved car for your group. Dzongu is easier: you can reach Mangan by shared jeep and your homestay can help with the permit.

No. Foreign nationals are not permitted at Gurudongmar Lake or Zero Point, and OCI card holders should confirm their own status with the operator. With a Protected Area Permit arranged by a registered agent, foreigners can visit Lachung, Yumthang and Lachen in a group of at least two. Rules have shifted before, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit North Sikkim?
faqs.a: April and May for rhododendrons in Yumthang and a thawing Gurudongmar, and October to November for clear skies and dry roads. December to March brings snow at Zero Point but closures are common on the Gurudongmar road. June to early September is monsoon: landslides are frequent and permits are often suspended.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a real risk here?
faqs.a: Yes. Lachung and Lachen are about 2,700 m, Yumthang 3,564 m, Zero Point about 4,700 m and Gurudongmar about 5,430 m. Spend a night at Lachen or Lachung before going higher, drink water, avoid alcohol, and come down at once if you get a bad headache, vomiting or confusion. People with heart or lung conditions should consult a doctor before going above 4,000 m.

faqs.q: Are the roads open after the 2023 Teesta flood?
faqs.a: The flood of October 2023 damaged bridges and long sections of road around Chungthang, and North Sikkim was closed to tourists for long periods afterwards. Access has since reopened in stages, but landslides keep causing closures, especially in the monsoon. Ask your operator on the day of booking and again the day before you leave. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a North Sikkim trip cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively, a two-night shared group tour from Gangtok to Lachung costs about ₹5,000–7,500 per person with basic rooms and meals. A reserved car for two nights runs about ₹14,000–19,000 per vehicle, plus hotels. Zero Point is an extra ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle. Prices rise in April, May and October.

faqs.q: Is there mobile signal and ATM access?
faqs.a: Signal is patchy. BSNL and Jio usually work in parts of Lachung and Lachen, while Airtel is weaker; expect no signal at Yumthang, Zero Point or Gurudongmar. Mangan has ATMs, but carry enough cash from Gangtok for tips, snow gear hire, tea stalls and extras, as cards are rarely accepted in the high villages.

faqs.q: Is North Sikkim suitable for children and older travellers?
faqs.a: Lachung and Yumthang suit most healthy families. Gurudongmar is a different matter: at 5,430 m, operators and doctors generally advise against taking small children, and older travellers with heart, lung or blood pressure problems should take medical advice first. The long drives on rough roads are also tiring, so build in rest.
